summary: Discovery focused on air-gapped on-prem lifecycle: firmware signing, offline update media, validation, rollback, and hardware constraints (GPUs/storage). Atlas needs a deterministic, auditable update path to meet regulator expectations. Redwood SEs explained private deployment packaging, signed-image mechanisms, and patterns for airgap update orchestration. Open questions remain on CA trust, HSM integration, and exact maintenance windows.
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Patel: all right good afternoon everyone, thanks for joining. quick intros — i'm jordan, i'm the AE partnering with atlas for the private deployment path.
[00:06] Dr. Nina Shah: nina here, head of it. we run the lab cluster and will need to make sure anything we install meets our validation process.
[00:12] Marcus Lee: infra lead, hi. i've got questions about gpu types and whether you support hermetic updates.
[00:18] Alicia Gomez: hey all, i'm alicia on the se side — i'll walk through how redwood's private package and the signed-image flow looks.
[00:24] Ravi Menon: ravi, embedded systems. we control firmware signing and secure boot; curious how you hand off artifacts.
[00:31] Jordan Patel: high level goal today: confirm we can do an air-gapped / offline update lifecycle with signed images, match atlas's CA/trust requirements, and understand hw constraints.
[00:40] Alicia Gomez: i can start. our private delivery is a customer-managed control plane. we produce a releases bundle — think tarball with model weights, runtime binaries, and a manifest that is cryptographically signed. in airgap mode customers bring the bundle via removable media or an approved staging server. the runtime validates signatures before install.
[00:58] Ravi Menon: when you say "cryptographically signed" — is that a certificate we provide, or do you sign it and we trust redwood?
[01:04] Alicia Gomez: good question. we support multiple patterns: by default redwood signs release bundles with our distro key for hosted customers; for private airgapped deployments we can ship unsigned artifacts and provide tooling so you sign locally with your CA, or we can coordinate a co-sign model where both signatures are present. the runtime checks the chain against a trust store you control.
[01:26] Evelyn Torres: for compliance we need key provenance. we use an HSM (AWS CloudHSM for some, on-prem HSM for others) and require that signing keys never leave the HSM. can your process integrate with an external HSM?
[01:36] Samir Rao: yes, we have an integration pattern — our packaging CLI can be pointed to a signing endpoint that proxies to an HSM. we also support offline signing: you can export the manifest, sign it on an airgapped machine with your HSM, and then ingest the signed bundle. the important part is that the runtime enforces the signature and logs the verification result to the audit log.
[01:56] Marcus Lee: storage footprint — what's the typical disk requirement for a model node? our constrained racks have NVMe pools and some older SATA disks — just want to size.
[02:04] Alicia Gomez: depends on model. a small Llama-2-7B-ish tuned model with quantization might be 10-15GB, while a 70B with KV cache can be hundreds. for inference nodes with GPU we recommend local NVMe for KV cache; we can run with networked storage but latency spikes if it's NFS on SATA.
[02:24] Ravi Menon: our hardware procurement includes H100s and a handful of A10s we keep as fallback, and some nodes are older with 32GB VRAM. does redwood runtime have automatic fallback to quantized variants for lower-VRAM GPUs?
[02:33] Samir Rao: yes, runtime supports model variants and fallback policies — we can route requests to a quantized/optimised variant when a node reports lower VRAM. for private deployments the mapping is in the policy file you control.
[02:44] Dr. Nina Shah: about update windows — regulators require a documented maintenance window and rollback plan. how do you handle failed installs?
[02:51] Alicia Gomez: our installer performs a pre-check: signature verification, checksum, and a dry-run of file system layout. the installer writes new artifacts to a separate path and only flips symlink on successful verification. rollback is immediate: if healthchecks fail post-flip, the service reverts to previous symlink. we also emit detailed logs that include signature thumbprints for audit.
[03:12] Marcus Lee: heartburn is networkless approval workflow. we have a process where change control must review the exact bundle; we need a human-in-loop sign-off before installation. do you have a play for that?
[03:21] Jordan Patel: yes, that's common. recommended pattern: redwood gives you the artifact bundle + manifest hash through a secure channel (s3 presigned or secure transfer). atlas downloads to an airgapped signing workstation, your change board signs the manifest (or co-signs) and returns the signed bundle on removable media. then install follows.
[03:38] Ravi Menon: how are revoked keys handled? if a CA is compromised and we need to revoke a signing cert, how does the runtime know?
[03:44] Samir Rao: the runtime shipping includes a trust store and a CRL/OCSP mechanism, but in airgapped mode you manage CRL distribution. we provide tooling to stamp a revocation list into the trust store at bundle ingestion time. we also support a "grace period" policy so you can control rollout across nodes.
[04:00] Evelyn Torres: audit trail is critical. we need tamper evidence and immutable logs. can logs be exported to our SIEM, and what about signed logs?
[04:07] Alicia Gomez: logs are local by default and include verification events; we support signed audit bundles and can produce an attest statement for each release install. customers typically ship these signed audit bundles via secure media to their central SIEM ingest. for central collection inside an airgapped site we can integrate with your on-prem log collector over internal network.
[04:24] Dr. Nina Shah: do you offer a validation harness? our QA wants to run known prompts and check model drift after each update.
[04:29] Samir Rao: yes, redwood optimize includes an eval harness; for private deployments we can provide the eval runner as part of the bundle so QA can run deterministic prompts pre/post-install. results are hashed and included in the install attest if you want.
[04:44] Marcus Lee: i'm worried about the firmware/driver surface — OS kernel modules, GPU drivers — will redwood package those or do we manage drivers separately?
[04:51] Alicia Gomez: we recommend customers manage base OS and drivers. redwood packages runtime binaries that expect a compatible driver ABI. for full-stack managed options we can provide a driver image but in highly regulated labs you often want to control kernel/drivers in change control. we can document required driver versions and provide a compatibility matrix.
[05:08] Ravi Menon: license and export controls — our legal team will need clarity on binaries in the bundle. are models precompiled or do you deliver weights?
[05:15] Jordan Patel: we deliver both depending on agreement: typically weights and a runtime. for some curated models we ship optimized binaries. we'll include license metadata in the manifest.
[05:24] Evelyn Torres: can we enforce RBAC for who can generate a signed bundle? for compliance we need separation of duties.
[05:29] Samir Rao: yes, the signing workflow can be restricted. the packaging CLI requires privileges and we integrate with your internal SSO/AD for who can upload artifacts to the staging server. the actual HSM signing step happens in your environment.
[05:40] Dr. Nina Shah: any automated fingerprinting to detect tampering after deploy?
[05:44] Alicia Gomez: runtime performs an integrity check on startup and periodically; if a file fails checksum it alerts and quarantines the node. we can configure watchdogs to isolate the node from load balancers.
[05:55] Jordan Patel: quick recap — agreed items: atlas will pull an example unsigned bundle, run local signing with their HSM, and we will observe an install in a lab node. redwood will provide the sample manifest, install runbook, and compatibility matrix.
[06:07] Marcus Lee: timeline — we prefer a bench test next week, pending internal procurement windows.
[06:11] Jordan Patel: great. i'll circulate next steps and will attach the runbook + sample signed bundle by tuesday. any last compliance questions?
[06:19] Evelyn Torres: please include a short note on SOC2 evidence and whether the signed bundle process aligns with FIPS expectations for hashing.
[06:26] Samir Rao: will do — we'll include hashing algorithms and recommended FIPS modes.
[06:31] Jordan Patel: thanks everyone — we'll follow up with dates.
[06:33] Dr. Nina Shah: thanks all. bye.
[06:35] [end of recording]
